youtube.title: This Coin Flip Isn't 50/50 #Shorts
youtube.description:
Last slice of pizza. One coin. Zoe knows something her brother doesn't.

A coin flip isn't quite 50/50. In a study of 350,757 flips by 48 people (every session filmed), a flipped-and-caught coin landed on the same side it started on about 50.8% of the time. The reason: a flipped coin wobbles as it spins, so it spends a little more of its flight with the starting side facing up. Heads vs tails on its own made no difference, and some flippers showed no bias at all - but over a thousand bets, calling the side facing up comes out ahead.

Would you call the side facing up?

Sources:
- Bartos et al., Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started: Evidence from 350,757 flips (arXiv 2310.04153; Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04153
- University of Amsterdam news: https://www.uva.nl/en/content/news/news/2023/10/heads-or-tails-pure-chance.html
- Utrecht University research portal: https://research-portal.uu.nl/en/publications/fair-coins-tend-to-land-on-the-same-side-they-started-evidence-fr/

Zoe, Leo and the pizza night are fictional.
